lead: The Hilbert transform is a filter that keeps every frequency's amplitude and shifts its phase by 90°. Positive frequencies get −90°; negative frequencies get +90°. In time, it turns cos(ω₀t) into sin(ω₀t). It exists because many systems need a quadrature copy of a signal: a version delayed by a quarter period. Single-sideband radio, envelope detection and instantaneous-frequency measurement use it. The same operation builds the analytic signal x(t)+jx̂(t). Some syllabi list it as an advanced Fourier-transform topic.
prereq: You need: the cosine Fourier transform pair and the phase-response idea from Chapter 3.2 and Chapter 3.5, plus the signum function.

blocks.text: The Hilbert transform of a real signal x(t) is another real signal x̂(t), read “x hat”:

blocks.where: x(t) is the input signal; x̂(t) is its Hilbert transform; τ is the integration time; t is the output time; PV means Cauchy principal value, which takes equal limits on both sides of the singularity at τ=t and cancels the infinite parts.

blocks.text: The Hilbert transformer is an LTI system. Its frequency response is H<sub>H</sub>(ω)=−j sgn(ω). The term sgn(ω) is the signum function: +1 for ω>0, 0 at ω=0, and −1 for ω<0. So |H<sub>H</sub>(ω)|=1 for every ω≠0. The phase is ∠H<sub>H</sub>(ω)=−90° for ω>0 and +90° for ω<0. At ω=0 the response is zero.

This is an all-pass filter with a quadrature phase shift. It does not change the size of any frequency component; it only moves positive-frequency components back by a quarter period and negative-frequency components forward by a quarter period. That is why a cosine becomes a sine, not a scaled cosine. The impulse response is h(t)=1/(πt), which is non-causal; an ideal Hilbert transformer cannot be built exactly in real time.
Five properties follow from H<sub>H</sub>(ω)=−j sgn(ω).

items: Linearity: H{a x₁(t)+b x₂(t)}=a H{x₁(t)}+b H{x₂(t)} for constants a and b.
Energy preservation: ∫|x̂(t)|²dt = ∫|x(t)|²dt. The reason is |H<sub>H</sub>(ω)|=1 at all ω≠0; the zero at ω=0 has zero area.
Orthogonality: for a real finite-energy signal x(t), ∫ x(t)x̂(t)dt=0. The two signals are 90° apart in phase, so their product has zero average.
Double transform: H{H{x(t)}}=−x(t) for a signal with no DC component. Squaring the frequency response gives (−j sgn ω)²=−1 for ω≠0. A DC term is removed by the first transform and cannot return.

Transform pairs for ω₀>0: cos(ω₀t) → sin(ω₀t) and sin(ω₀t) → −cos(ω₀t). The arrow means “Hilbert transform of”. The sign comes from multiplying the positive-frequency term by −j, which is a −90° rotation.

blocks.text: Analytic signal, in one line: x<sub>a</sub>(t)=x(t)+j x̂(t), with j=√−1. For x(t)=cos(ω₀t), x<sub>a</sub>(t)=cos(ω₀t)+j sin(ω₀t)=exp(jω₀t), so it contains only the positive frequency ω₀. This complex signal is the starting point for envelope and instantaneous-frequency ideas; those applications are outside this chapter.

figure.caption: The cosine and its Hilbert transform are 90° apart; at ω₀t=π/2 the cosine is 0 and the sine is +1, showing the −90° shift for positive frequency.

spec.aria: The Hilbert transform of a cosine is a sine, which is a −90° phase shift in this plot.

examples.question: A signal x(t)=cos(2t), with t in seconds, passes through an ideal Hilbert transformer. Using the exp(−jωt) Fourier convention, find x̂(t) and x̂(1 s).
steps: The Fourier transform of cos(2t) is X(ω)=π[δ(ω−2)+δ(ω+2)].
The Hilbert frequency response is H<sub>H</sub>(ω)=−j sgn(ω). At ω=2, sgn(2)=+1, so H<sub>H</sub>(2)=−j. At ω=−2, sgn(−2)=−1, so H<sub>H</sub>(−2)=+j.
Take the inverse transform: x̂(t)=(1/2π)[−jπ exp(j2t)+jπ exp(−j2t)]=sin(2t).
examples.answer: x̂(t)=sin(2t); at t=1 s, x̂(1)=0.9093 (dimensionless amplitude).
examples.check:
import math
omega0 = 2.0
t = 1.0
xhat = math.sin(omega0 * t)
print(round(xhat, 4))

traps: Choosing the sign of the 90° shift. Under the exp(−jωt) convention, H{cos(ω₀t)}=+sin(ω₀t), not −sin(ω₀t).
Forgetting that the Hilbert transformer has zero response at ω=0. A DC term is removed, so H{H{x}}=−x only for zero-mean signals.
Swapping the sine pair. For ω₀>0, H{sin(ω₀t)}=−cos(ω₀t).
Thinking the Hilbert transform turns a real signal into a complex one. The transform x̂(t) is real; the analytic signal x(t)+jx̂(t) is the complex one.
Using magnitude 1 at every frequency and ignoring the phase. The magnitude is flat, but the phase is the whole operation.

quiz.q: Write the frequency response of the ideal Hilbert transformer and give its magnitude and phase.
quiz.a: H<sub>H</sub>(ω)=−j sgn(ω). |H<sub>H</sub>|=1 for ω≠0, phase −90° for ω>0 and +90° for ω<0; the response is zero at ω=0.

quiz.q: Why does a cosine become a sine rather than a scaled cosine?
quiz.a: The Hilbert transformer multiplies the positive-frequency component by −j, a −90° phase shift, and the magnitude stays 1. Only phase changes, so cos becomes sin.

quiz.q: Find the Hilbert transform of x(t)=sin(3t).
quiz.a: Here ω₀=3>0. The pair is H{sin(ω₀t)}=−cos(ω₀t). So x̂(t)=−cos(3t).

quiz.q: Show from the frequency response that the Hilbert transform preserves signal energy.
quiz.a: By Parseval, energy of x̂ is (1/2π)∫|X(ω)|²|H<sub>H</sub>(ω)|²dω. Since |H<sub>H</sub>(ω)|²=1 for ω≠0, this equals (1/2π)∫|X(ω)|²dω, the energy of x.

quiz.q: Define the analytic signal of a real signal x(t).
quiz.a: x<sub>a</sub>(t)=x(t)+j x̂(t), where x̂(t) is the Hilbert transform and j=√−1.

quiz.q: Does H{H{x}}=−x hold for x(t)=5+cos(2t)? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The first Hilbert transform removes the DC term 5 and gives sin(2t). The second gives −cos(2t), not −5−cos(2t).

quiz.q: For x(t)=cos(5t), find the analytic signal x<sub>a</sub>(t).

beyond: Not for the exam. Single-sideband radio uses the Hilbert transform to cancel one sideband. Quadrature receivers use the 90° phase shift to separate I and Q channels. In research, the analytic signal gives instantaneous amplitude and frequency for vibration monitoring and speech analysis. Search next for “analytic signal”, “Hilbert transform SSB” and “quadrature demodulation”.
